abstract_summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-session tools toward long-term personal assistants that must adapt to individual users across tasks, contexts, and interactions. This shift makes memory a core requirement for personalization, since user preferences, goals, constraints, relationships, and pa...

Our contributions are as follows:
•Taxonomy. We develop a lifecycle taxonomy that or-
ganizes existing studies on graph-based personalized
memory around representation, evolution, retrieval, and
evaluation.
•Evaluation. We summarize existing benchmarks and
metrics and identify gaps in graph quality, user control,
lifecycle validity, and realistic personalization.
•Timely Review. For each category, we review recent
methods and discuss their motivations, graph structures,
and user-modeling functions.
•Future Directions. We outline several open research
directions to guide future research on this promising
topic.
II. PRELIMINARIES
A. Graph-based Personalized Memory
Personalization refers to an LLM agent adapting its re-
sponses, retrieval, and actions to an individual user.

evidence.excerpt:
tests long-horizon
conversational recall. LoCoMo [52] is a common evaluation
benchmark for graph-memory papers, including production-
ready memory with a graph variant [31], topology-aware
graph reasoning [41], learned traversal [53], multi-scale user
memory [54], and graph-native versioned memory [45]. Long-
MemEval [55] evaluates longer histories, knowledge updates,
single-session preference questions, temporal reasoning, and
abstention. These benchmarks are valuable because they force
retrieval under multi-session noise, but they mostly observe
whether the final answer is correct rather than whether the
memory graph itself is correct.
Personalization-specific benchmarks shift the target from
factual recall to user-state modeling. PersonaMem [56]
tests dynamic user-profile and preference tracking, while
PersonaMem-v2 [9] scales this setting to implicit personas,
longer contexts, 
[… separate evidence block …]
ActMemEval [62]
tests whether retrieved memory supports implicit con-
straint and counterfactual reasoning, while ATM-Bench [63]
adds multimodal, multi-source personal evidence. Struct-
MemEval [64] asks whether memory is organized correctly.
Across these benchmarks, reported metrics fall into five
groups:
•Answer quality:F1, exact match, multiple-choice accu-
racy, task success, and LLM-as-judge score.
•Evidence retrieval:Recall@k, NDCG@k, answer-turn
retrieval accuracy, evidence-location accuracy, and mul-
timodal evidence recall.
•User-state modeling:preference-category accuracy, pro-
file or persona consistency, and correctness or helpfulness
of personalized responses.
•Memory evolution and structure:update success, step
or chain accuracy under changing environments, forget-
ting/update outcomes, structure-requiring task accuracy,
and failure-attribution

The challenges section then identifies gaps in graph quality, user control, lifecycle validity, and realistic personalization, fulfilling the stated evaluation contribution.

positive_signals: The paper's stated contribution is a lifecycle-oriented taxonomy organizing graph-based personalized memory for LLM agents around representation, evolution, retrieval, and evaluation.
The survey fills a gap by providing a unified account of graph-based personalized memory across representation, evolution, retrieval, and evaluation, which prior surveys do not provide.
The survey summarizes existing benchmarks and metrics for personalized memory and identifies gaps in graph quality, user control, lifecycle validity, and realistic personalization.
The survey's claims about representation patterns, evolution operations, and retrieval mechanisms are grounded in named systems with specific design descriptions.

The paper positions itself against prior surveys of personalized agents, graph-based agent memory, and broader agent-memory surveys, arguing that none provides a unified lifecycle account of graph-based personalized memory.
The survey maintains a continuously updated public repository of the reviewed literature.

The survey acknowledges open evaluation questions and limitations of specific design patterns, such as the unverified generality of multiple disjoint graphs and the unresolved reliability of dependency propagation.
The survey uses a consistent, well-defined vocabulary for its taxonomy, including explicit definitions of memory dimensions, node roles, relation functions, and representation patterns.
